children.text: A Kankanaey village in the Cordillera mountains about

above sea level, famous for its unique burial custom of hanging coffins on cliffs and its huge limestone caves. Sea-of-clouds sunrises at Marlboro Hills, pine forests, cool weather, and a laid-back cafe culture draw backpackers.
Sagada is a village set in limestone highlands about

above sea level, in the western part of Mountain Province. Home for generations to the Kankanaey (Applai) people, it was connected to the outside world in the early 20th century when American Episcopal missionaries arrived and built schools and a church, and it remains a distinctive community today where the Episcopal church and traditional beliefs coexist.
Sagada is a small municipality of 19 barangays covering 83.32 km², with 10,702 residents as of the
census. Its rugged mountains kept outside influence to a minimum even in the Spanish era, and a mission outpost was not established until
. In

, an American Episcopal mission led by Father John Staunton founded St. Mary's Church and St. Mary's School, and today Sagada is a rare town in the Philippines where most residents belong to the Episcopal Church in the Philippines. Photographer Eduardo Masferré, who documented the lives of Cordillera people, came from here, and historian William Henry Scott also lived here and was buried in the church cemetery in

What put Sagada on the map was its "hanging coffins." The custom comes from the belief that hanging an ancestor's body on a cliff, closer to the sky, lets the soul travel higher, and old wooden coffins still hang from the rock face at Echo Valley today. Besides the hanging coffins, there are several burial caves where coffins are stacked at the cave entrance, offering a direct look at how Cordillera people view death.

The terrain is another draw. Huge caves, formed as rainwater dissolved the limestone, run beneath the village, and at Sumaguing Cave you can explore with a guide, climbing up and down the rocks barefoot and crossing underground pools. This whole area was once seabed long ago, so you can even spot fossil shells on the walls of Sumaguing Cave. At dawn, a sea of clouds fills the valleys around Marlboro Hills and Kiltepan, and by day you can enjoy waterfall treks through rice terraces and pine forests.
The

Filipino film That Thing Called Tadhana ends here, which also made Sagada famous as a destination for couples and young travelers. It's especially recommended for backpackers who want a quiet mountain-village atmosphere, laid-back cafes, and adventure activities all at once, and for anyone interested in Philippine indigenous culture.

blocks.title: Echo Valley and the hanging coffins

children.text: Pass the cemetery behind the village's Episcopal church and walk down a forest trail for
20–30 minutes
to see the coffins hanging on the cliff. A guide is required, and there is also a route continuing down to the valley below the cliff.
Sagada's largest cave, where over about
2 hours
you hold onto ropes to climb down the rocks and cross cold underground pools. Huge stalagmites and named rock formations such as the "Crown" and the "Turtle" are impressive.
A
3–4 hour

route that enters through Lumiang Burial Cave, where coffins are stacked, and exits at Sumaguing Cave. There are sections where you crawl through narrow gaps and wade through water, requiring both stamina and nerve, but it's rated Sagada's best adventure.

blocks.title: Sea-of-clouds sunrise on the Kiltepan road

children.text: The summit viewpoint at Kiltepan, once Sagada's best-known spot for the sea of clouds, has been closed to tourists since a fire in
November 2018

. These days, visitors watch the clouds over an etag sandwich and coffee at 1sangwow Cafe by the Clouds along the Kiltepan road, or climb Marlboro Hills with a guide. The chance of a sea of clouds is highest at dawn in
November–February
A waterfall about
high, reached by a walk of about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes
past the rice terraces of Fidelisan village. The village scenery seen along the paddy paths is as beautiful as the waterfall itself.

A trek that passes through pine forest to watch the sunrise from the grassy hilltop of Marlboro Hills, then descends to the Blue Soil Hills, where bluish earth lies exposed. Take a shuttle to the trailhead around
4 AM
, climb for about
1 hour
to watch the sunrise, then walk down to Blue Soil; the whole trip takes
4–5 hours
. The guide fee is about
per group, and the shuttle is paid separately.
A small lake surrounded by pine forest on the edge of the village, good for a quiet stroll around sunset. It lies about
4km
west of the village along the Sagada–Besao road, roughly
1 hour
on foot, so set out early enough to arrive at least
30 minutes
before sunset.
At the workshops you can browse and buy Sagada pottery, fired the traditional way, and Cordillera textiles. At Sagada Weaving, founded by Andrea Bondad in
, you can watch weavers making cloth on looms (ask permission before taking photos), and the pottery workshop is on the way to Danum Lake, so it's easy to visit both together.

A guide is mandatory on the Marlboro Hills route, and the shuttle costs extra. Mountain trails before dawn are dark and slippery with dew, so bring a headlamp and shoes with good grip.

Coda Lines runs a daily direct overnight bus from Cubao in Manila to Sagada via Banaue and Bontoc. The trip takes about
11–13 hours
, and fares are about
depending on seat class. Seats are limited, so book ahead for weekends and holidays.
The Cubao terminal is at the corner of Monte de Piedad Street and Maryland Street (near the HM Transport terminal). According to the Sagada Tourism Office, there are 2–4 evening departures a day (
), and the 35-seat buses with restrooms cost slightly more than the 45-seat buses. You can book online through Bookaway.
Return Coda Lines buses leave the stop in Sagada town in the afternoon (
) and reach Cubao late at night or before dawn.
Travel from Manila to Baguio by bus, about
4–6 hours
, then take a bus to Sagada (GL Trans, Lizardo Trans, and others) from near the Dangwa terminal in Baguio. Following Halsema Highway, it takes about
5–6 hours
, for a fare of about
Halsema Highway is a mountain road running about
150km
from Baguio to Bontoc, climbing to about
above sea level at Atok, Benguet. It was the highest national highway in the Philippines until a road in Tinoc, Ifugao, was confirmed to be higher in
. The road is full of curves, so it's a good idea to bring motion-sickness medicine.
The Sagada Tourism Office lists GL Trans departures from Baguio at
, and
. Tickets can't be booked in advance and must be bought in person at the Dangwa terminal behind Center Mall, so head there early on weekends.
From Banaue to Bontoc it's about
2–3 hours
by van or jeepney, and from Bontoc to Sagada about
1 hour
by jeepney. This is convenient for combining with a Banaue and Batad itinerary.
Bontoc–Sagada jeepneys run mainly from the morning until early afternoon, with fares of about
. If you arrive late, you'll have to charter a vehicle in Bontoc, so try to make the transfer in the morning.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK), and going via Baguio takes about
8–10 hours
in total. Bus travel is essentially the default way in.

The village center is walkable. For Lumiang and Sumaguing caves, Marlboro Hills, and Bomod-ok Falls, hire a chartered van (shuttle) near the tourist information center; each route has a fixed rate (about
per van).
Guided sites often require you to use the shuttle as well, so when you book a guide at the tourist information center, book the shuttle at the same time.

There are three main driving routes from Manila: via Baguio along Halsema Highway; up through Nueva Vizcaya and Ifugao (Banaue) to Bontoc; and the western route climbing from the Ilocos Sur coast through Cervantes.
The Sagada Tourism Office advises against driving the mountain roads at night, when fog cuts visibility. In the rainy season (
June–October
), watch out for landslides, and fill up your tank before setting off. Parking in town is very limited, so check in advance whether your lodging has parking.
The dry season,
November–April
, is the best time to travel.
December–February
is the coldest stretch, with dawn temperatures sometimes dropping below

, but the chance of a sea of clouds is high and the air is clear, giving you the quintessential Sagada scenery. This is also when Sagada oranges are in season, so you can taste fresh oranges around the village.
March–May
is warm and clear, but tourists crowd in during Holy Week and the summer break, sometimes leaving accommodation and guides in short supply.
During the rainy season,
June–October
, rain is frequent and fog is thick. After heavy rain, the caves can flood and the Connection route may be suspended, and landslides on Halsema Highway can block traffic. Around All Saints' Day on
November 1
, you can see villagers gather at the cemetery to light candles in remembrance, but since this is a community event, you should observe it quietly.
Village festivals and community events can also affect your plans. Every year from
late January to early February

, the Etag Festival honors the traditional smoked pork with folk dance competitions and a farmers' market selling coffee and vegetables. On "ubaya" days, when the village rests after planting, after harvest, or after a disaster, sites such as Bomod-ok Falls close, and on
December 1, 2025
, Echo Valley, Sumaguing Cave, and Bokong Falls closed for a day for the annual community gathering "sagangsang." Average annual rainfall is about 2,835 mm, most of it falling in
May–October

Guesthouses and small inns cluster in the village center, around the tourist information center and bus stop. Options range from simple rooms at about
per night to lodging with pine forest views at around
. Air conditioning isn't needed, but since nights are cold, check whether hot water and thick blankets are provided. Booking ahead of arrival is safer during peak season.

For such a small village, Sagada has a rich food culture. Signature items include the lemon pie from the longtime landmark "Lemon Pie House," handmade yogurt and granola from the Yoghurt House, dishes made with the region's traditional smoked pork "etag," and locally grown Arabica coffee. Some restaurants known for their dinner buffets operate by reservation, so book a table earlier in the day. Shops tend to close by around
8–9 PM
To name a few well-known places: Sagada Lemon Pie House, which started baking lemon pies to sell at the market in
and opened as a restaurant in

, is known for its lemon pie and egg pie, while the Yoghurt House on the main road is famous for yogurt topped with granola and bananas and its all-day breakfast. Gaia Cafe, overlooking the rice terraces, serves vegetarian dishes. Sagada coffee descends from the Arabica coffee the Spanish introduced in
, so the beans make a great souvenir, and locally grown Sagada oranges (ponkan) and vacuum-packed etag are also popular gifts.
As soon as you arrive, register at the tourist information center first and get your environmental fee receipt. This receipt is checked at the entrance to every attraction.
Most attractions require an accredited guide by rule. Book one at the tourist information center or the guides' association office at the set rate.
On the day of your cave exploration, bring clothes that can get wet, sandals or aqua shoes, and a change of clothes and towel. There are stretches inside the caves where you walk barefoot.
There are only one or two ATMs in Sagada village, and they often run out of cash. Withdraw plenty of cash in Baguio or Bontoc beforehand.
During holidays, traffic piles up on the way to the dawn sea-of-clouds viewpoints. Leave around
4 AM
, or for nearby spots such as the cafes along the Kiltepan road, consider walking.
Temperatures drop sharply at night. Bring a light padded jacket, long pants, and socks.
When taking photos, always ask permission before photographing residents, especially elders, or any ritual scenes.
To avoid the queue at the tourist information center, register before you arrive with the
Sagada iPass online registration

run by the Sagada municipality and get your QR pass. Paid bookings are non-refundable and non-transferable, and the date can be changed only for typhoons or road closures. Children aged 7 and under do not need to register.

Each guide can take only a set number of people (about 4 for Sumaguing Cave, about 10 for Echo Valley and Bomod-ok Falls). If you're traveling alone or as a pair, team up with other travelers at the tourist information center and split the guide and shuttle fees to save a lot.
You can find accredited lodgings, guides, and tour operators in the list on the
Sagada Tourism Office official website
, and notices such as temporary site closures are also posted on the tourism office's Facebook page (Sagadatourism).

The hanging coffins and burial caves are the graves of local ancestors before they are tourist attractions. Touching the coffins, moving bones, or climbing on top of the graves to take photos is absolutely forbidden.
Sagada strictly limits late-night noise and public drinking by local ordinance. Stay quiet at night even at your accommodation.
The Cave Connection route has slippery rocks and deep water, carrying a risk of accidents. Never enter without a guide.
Landslides are frequent on Halsema Highway and mountain roads during the rainy season. Check road conditions before traveling and build in a flexible schedule.
During peak season, visitor numbers may be capped or certain attractions temporarily closed, so check the tourist information center's latest notices.
Motion sickness can be severe on the mountain bus ride, so avoid traveling on an empty stomach and bring motion-sickness medicine.
Beware of unlicensed tour arrangers selling cheap packages online. In
August 2025

, the Sagada municipality suspended the operations of tour arrangers and travel agencies involved in fraud and false advertising, such as using photos of other lodgings. It's safest to book lodging and tours directly with operators accredited by the tourism office.
